title: Customer Service and Retail Banking Excellence
subtitle: Serve every customer with respect, know the retail products, explain costs clearly and handle complaints by the rules
summary: Build the service skills and retail product knowledge that Ethiopian branches need, from busy salary-day queues to remittance payouts and complaints, using one Addis Ababa branch as a running case.
audience: Tellers, customer service officers and new branch staff in Ethiopian banks and microfinance institutions. No prerequisites.
objectives: Describe the bank's retail products and the customer journey through a branch
Deliver courteous, accurate and compliant service, including to vulnerable customers
Explain fees, rates and the annual percentage rate in plain words and Birr amounts
Handle complaints according to the NBE's consumer protection expectations and the bank's procedures
Apply KYC, cash handling, counterfeit, confidentiality and fraud rules at the counter

runningCase.name: Bank A, Kera branch
runningCase.text: Bank A's Kera branch in Addis Ababa is a fictional busy branch near a market and several factories, with 6 teller windows, 2 customer service desks and 1 ATM. On salary days the hall fills before opening. You join as new customer service officer Hanna Girma, working with teller Dawit Alemu, senior customer service officer Meron Haile and branch manager Tigist Bekele. Across the five modules you meet ten common branch moments: queue frustration, a trader choosing between a wallet and an account, a pensioner puzzled by a fee, a loan rejection, a remittance payout without ID, a wheelchair user at the steps, a counterfeit note, a caller asking for a spouse's balance, a failed transfer and an angry customer whose card the ATM captured. The capstone tests all ten as role plays scored with a service rubric.

modules.title: The service mindset and the branch customer journey
modules.summary: Understand why service decides who wins in a crowded Ethiopian banking market, and walk the customer's path through a busy branch from the door to the goodbye.
objectives: Explain why service quality matters more as banks, mobile money and new entrants compete for the same customers
Apply Ethiopian norms of respect, greeting and language to first impressions at the branch
Map the customer journey through a branch and name the moments of truth at each stage
Estimate how teller capacity and service time drive queues, and suggest practical fixes

lessons.title: Why service matters in a competitive market
body: Ethiopian customers now have more choices than at any time before. Many banks open branches on the same street, mobile money wallets move money without a branch visit, and the new Banking Business Proclamation opens the door to foreign banks. When accounts, rates and fees look alike, the experience at the counter is often the only real difference a customer feels.

Good service is also good business. A customer who is treated well brings salary, savings and a family's accounts, and recommends the branch to neighbors, the idir and the equb. A customer who is treated badly rarely complains to the bank. They tell ten people and quietly move their money.

Service is not only smiling. It is accuracy (the transaction is right the first time), speed (no wasted waiting), clarity (the customer understands what was done and what it cost) and fairness (every customer gets the same respect and the same rules).

items.label: Accuracy
items.text: Right the first time: amount, account, name.

items.label: Speed
items.text: No avoidable waiting, at the queue or the desk.

items.label: Clarity
items.text: The customer understands the product and the cost.

items.label: Fairness
items.text: Same respect and same rules for every customer.

example.title: Two branches on one street
example.text: Two banks have branches 50 meters apart near a busy market in Hawassa. Their savings rates differ by less than half a point. Over one year, the branch whose tellers greet traders by name, explain every fee and call back when a transfer is late grows its deposits by Birr 40 million. The other branch, with the same products, loses three large trader accounts after a single afternoon when a customer was told to 'come back tomorrow' without a reason.

lessons.title: Meet the running case: Bank A's Kera branch
body: Throughout this course you work at Bank A's Kera branch in Addis Ababa, a fictional busy branch near a market and several factories. On salary days the hall fills before the doors open. Customers include traders, factory workers, pensioners, students, diaspora families receiving remittances and small businesses.

You join as a new customer service officer, Hanna Girma. Your colleagues are teller Dawit Alemu, senior customer service officer Meron Haile and branch manager Tigist Bekele. In each module you meet some of the ten branch moments that the capstone role plays test, from queue frustration to a remittance payout without an ID.
Keep a notebook as you go. For each moment, write what the customer needs, what the rule says and what you would say. The final module turns these notes into role plays scored with a service rubric.
points: The branch has 6 teller windows, 2 customer service desks and 1 ATM
Busiest times: salary days, Monday mornings and the days before holidays
Main languages heard: Amharic, Afaan Oromo, Tigrigna and Gurage languages, with some English
lessons.tip: Learn the names of your colleagues' roles on day one, so you always know whom to call for an override, an exception or a complaint.

lessons.title: Ethiopian service culture, respect and first impressions
body: First impressions form in seconds. A customer reads your posture, your greeting and whether you looked up from the screen. In Ethiopian culture, respect is shown through a proper greeting, the respectful form of address and patience with elders. Use 'Ato', 'Weizero' or 'Weizerit' with the customer's name, and the polite form of 'you' in Amharic and other languages.

Greet the customer in the language they use, or ask politely which language they prefer. If you do not speak it, find a colleague who does instead of switching to a language the customer struggles with. Never laugh at an accent or a mistake in writing.

Appearance and the workspace also speak. A clean desk, a visible name badge, a working pen and forms within reach tell the customer they are expected. A teller eating at the window or chatting on a personal phone tells them the opposite.

items.label: Look up and smile
items.text: Stop what you are doing and make eye contact.

items.label: Greet respectfully
items.text: Use the greeting and form of address the customer expects.

items.label: Offer help
items.text: 'How may I help you today?' in the customer's language.

items.label: Listen to the request
items.text: Let the customer finish before you answer.

items.label: Confirm and act
items.text: Repeat the request in short, then serve.

scenario.title: The elder at the desk
scenario.situation: An elderly man in traditional dress approaches Hanna's desk while she is finishing an entry. He speaks Afaan Oromo and looks unsure. Hanna speaks only a little Afaan Oromo, and Meron, who is fluent, is at the next desk.
scenario.question: What is the best first response?
options: Keep typing and signal him to wait without looking up
Answer in English because it is the bank's official working language
Ask him to take a queue ticket and come back
Stand or look up, greet him respectfully, then ask Meron to help in Afaan Oromo
scenario.explain: A respectful greeting costs a few seconds and sets the tone; bringing in a colleague who speaks his language serves him properly. Ignoring him, switching to English or sending him away without help all damage trust.

lessons.title: The customer journey through a branch
body: A customer journey is every step a customer takes, from deciding to visit the branch to leaving it, and what they think and feel at each step. Looking at the branch through the customer's eyes shows problems staff no longer notice, such as a broken ticket machine or a form only available in one language.

Each stage has a 'moment of truth': a point where the customer decides whether the bank is reliable. For most branch customers, the moments of truth are the first greeting, the wait, the accuracy of the transaction and how a problem is handled. One failure can undo several good steps.
Front-line staff can improve most moments without new systems: guide customers to the right queue, check documents while they wait, explain the receipt and thank them by name.

items.label: Before the visit
items.text: Hears about the bank, checks opening hours, prepares documents.

items.label: Arrival
items.text: Security, greeter, queue ticket or directions to the right desk.

items.label: Waiting
items.text: Seating, screen or ticket calls, information on fees and products.

items.label: At the counter
items.text: Greeting, identification, the transaction, the receipt.

items.label: Leaving
items.text: Thanks, next step explained, digital channel offered for next time.

items.label: After the visit
items.text: SMS alert arrives, the transfer reaches the payee, a promised call-back happens.

example.title: The missing form
example.text: Kera branch staff walked the journey of a customer opening a savings account. They found that the account opening form was handed out only at the desk, so customers waited 25 minutes, then learned they needed a photo and a copy of their ID and had to come back. Placing a one-page checklist at the entrance in Amharic and Afaan Oromo, and letting the greeter hand out forms, cut return visits for missing documents by more than half in one month.

lessons.title: Queues: why they grow and what front-line staff can do
body: Long queues are the most common branch complaint in Ethiopia. A queue grows whenever customers arrive faster than the open windows can serve them. Two numbers drive it: how many customers arrive per hour, and how long each transaction takes.

Some causes are outside your control, such as a system outage. Many are not: windows closed for breaks at peak time, slow cash counting without machines, customers in the wrong queue, or transactions that could be done on mobile banking or the ATM. A greeter who sorts the queue and moves simple requests to digital channels can cut waiting time sharply.
When customers must wait, tell them honestly how long and why. People accept a wait they understand far more easily than one that feels unfair, such as staff serving acquaintances first.

worked.title: Kera branch, salary day, 8:00 to 10:00

rows.label: Customers one teller serves per hour (60 / 4)
Capacity with 4 windows at 3 minutes each (4 x 20)

worked.note: Opening all six windows at peak stops the queue from growing. Cutting service time to 3 minutes, for example by pre-filled slips and moving balance checks to the ATM, helps but is not enough on its own.

scenario.title: The payday break
scenario.situation: On salary day at 9:00 there are 45 people in the queue at Kera branch. Two of the six tellers ask to take their tea break together now, because they started early.
scenario.question: What should the branch manager decide?
options: Stagger the breaks to after the peak and ask the greeter to move balance enquiries to the ATM
Approve both breaks, since staff welfare comes first
Close the queue at 9:00 and ask the rest to return tomorrow
Approve the breaks and put up a sign apologizing for the delay
scenario.explain: Breaks still happen, but outside the peak, and the greeter reduces demand on the windows. Taking two windows out at peak would add about 30 customers to the queue per hour; closing the queue turns a delay into a refusal of service.

lessons.title: From mindset to a service promise
body: A service mindset means every staff member, not only customer service officers, sees the customer as the reason the branch exists. The guard who opens the door, the cleaner who keeps the hall tidy and the manager who handles an escalation all shape the experience.

Banks turn the mindset into a short service promise: a few standards everyone can remember and be checked against, such as greeting every customer, explaining every fee and calling back on every promise. A promise only works if it is measured and if staff are supported to keep it.
The law also expects fair treatment. The NBE's consumer protection mandate means that courtesy is not a favor to the customer; fair, clear and respectful treatment is part of the bank's obligation.

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025, Art. 41 (consumer protection)
regulation.text: The NBE Proclamation gives the National Bank a consumer protection role over the financial institutions it supervises. Together with the NBE's financial consumer protection directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported), this means banks must treat customers fairly, disclose terms clearly and give customers a way to complain. Front-line staff are where these duties are met or broken.

example.title: Kera branch's four promises
example.text: Tigist Bekele asked her team to agree four promises: greet every customer within one minute of reaching a desk; explain every fee before the customer signs; never say 'come back tomorrow' without a reason and a time; call back on the same day on every promise made. Each Friday, Meron checks ten transactions against the promises and shares the results with the team.

lessons.tip: If you cannot keep a promise, call the customer before the deadline, not after.

takeaways: When products look alike, the branch experience is often the customer's main reason to stay or leave.
Service means accuracy, speed, clarity and fairness, not only courtesy.
Respectful greetings, the right form of address and the customer's own language build trust in seconds.
Map the journey through the customer's eyes and fix the moments of truth: greeting, wait, accuracy and problem handling.
A queue grows when arrivals exceed window capacity; staff breaks, slow counting and wrong queues are usually fixable.

quiz.q: Which is the best description of good branch service?
options: Accuracy, speed, clarity and fairness in every transaction
Smiling at every customer
Serving important customers first
Selling as many products as possible
quiz.explain: Courtesy matters, but service is the whole experience: a correct, quick, clear and fair transaction.

quiz.q: A branch receives 80 customers per hour. Each teller serves 16 per hour. How many windows are needed to stop the queue growing?
quiz.explain: 80 / 16 = 5 windows; with fewer, the queue grows every hour.

quiz.q: What is a 'moment of truth' in the customer journey?
options: The moment the customer signs a form
The time the branch opens
The moment the bank checks the customer's ID
A point where the customer decides whether the bank is reliable
quiz.explain: Moments of truth, such as the greeting, the wait and problem handling, shape the customer's judgment of the bank.

quiz.q: A customer speaks Tigrigna and you do not. What should you do?
options: Speak slowly in Amharic until they understand
Greet them respectfully and ask a colleague who speaks Tigrigna to help
Ask them to return with a family member
Use English
quiz.explain: Serving customers in a language they understand is part of fair treatment.

quiz.q: Which action most directly reduces waiting time at peak hours without new systems?
options: Longer opening hours on Saturdays
Printing a new brochure
Staggering staff breaks outside the peak and moving simple requests to the ATM or mobile banking
Raising fees on counter transactions
quiz.explain: Keeping windows open at peak and reducing demand on them both work immediately.

quiz.q: Why do banks write a short service promise?
options: To replace NBE rules
To give staff a few clear standards that can be checked and kept
To advertise rates
To avoid handling complaints
quiz.explain: A promise turns the service mindset into standards everyone can remember and be measured against.

modules.title: Retail products and matching them to needs
modules.summary: Know the retail products a branch offers, from accounts and transfers to cards, mobile banking, loans, remittance payout and interest-free products, and recommend the one that fits the customer.
objectives: Describe the main deposit accounts and their features, including fixed time deposits and foreign currency accounts
Explain transfers, cards, mobile banking and remittance payout, and the limits that apply
Describe interest-free products offered under SBB/72/2019 and when a customer may prefer them
Match a product to a customer's need using a few simple questions

lessons.title: Deposit accounts: savings, current and fixed time
body: Most relationships start with a deposit account. A savings account keeps money safe, earns interest and allows withdrawals with a passbook or card. A current (checking) account is for people and businesses who pay by cheque; it needs a TIN and a check that the applicant is not on the list of delinquent cheque issuers. A fixed time deposit locks money for an agreed period at a higher rate, and interest is usually lost or reduced on early withdrawal.

Banks also offer special accounts for specific needs: children's trust accounts opened by a guardian, women's savings accounts, save-for-credit accounts, accounts for idir and equb groups, and pension or provident fund accounts. Minimum opening balances differ by bank; examples in one Ethiopian bank's procedures are Birr 25 for savings and Birr 250 for checking.

Since January 2026 each bank sets its own deposit rates, approved by its board. There is no longer an NBE minimum savings rate, so tell customers the bank's current rate and where it is published, and never promise a rate the bank has not set.

left.title: Savings account
items: Withdraw any time with passbook or card
Earns the bank's savings rate
Low opening balance
For salaries, household money, emergency funds

right.title: Fixed time deposit
items: Money locked for 3, 6, 12 months or more
Higher rate for the term
Written application and certificate
Interest lost or reduced if withdrawn early

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. NBE/INT/13/2026, Interest Rates (As Amended)
regulation.text: From 9 January 2026, each bank freely sets its demand, savings and time deposit rates and its lending rates. Rates must be approved in writing by the bank's board on written criteria and reported to the NBE. There is no NBE minimum savings rate, so staff quote the bank's own published rates.

worked.title: Fixed deposit for Weizero Almaz Kebede (illustrative rates)

rows.label: Illustrative fixed deposit rate set by the bank
Interest at maturity, before any tax (50,000 x 9%)
Illustrative savings rate set by the bank
Interest in savings over 12 months (50,000 x 7%)
Extra earned by fixing the deposit

worked.note: The fixed deposit earns more only if Almaz will not need the money for 12 months; if she may need part of it, split it between the two.

lessons.title: Transfers, cards and mobile banking
body: Customers move money in many ways: transfers within the bank, transfers to other banks through the national switch, cashier's payment orders for large or secure payments, debit cards for ATMs and point-of-sale machines, and mobile and internet banking for transfers, bill payments and balance checks.

Each channel has its own limits, fees and timing. A transfer within the bank is usually instant; a transfer to another bank may take longer or fail if the account details are wrong. Mobile money wallets run by payment instrument issuers are limited by the NBE: under ONPS/09/2023, a wallet may hold up to Birr 75,000 at any time and send up to Birr 150,000 a day in total, with some exemptions.

Helping a customer move routine transactions to mobile banking or the ATM saves them a trip and frees the counter for transactions that need a person. Always show them how to use the channel safely: never share the PIN or a one-time code, and check the payee's name before confirming.

items.label: Branch transfer
items.text: Within the bank or to another bank, with a slip or request.

items.label: Cashier's payment order
items.text: Secure payment for property, tenders, large amounts.

items.label: Debit card
items.text: ATM cash and payments at POS machines.

items.label: Mobile banking
items.text: Transfers, bills, airtime and balance at any time.

items.label: ATM
items.text: Cash and balance checks outside banking hours.

items.label: POS and QR
items.text: Payments at shops without cash.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. ONPS/09/2023, Payment Instrument Issuer (Amendment)
regulation.text: The directive raised the daily wallet balance limit for mobile money from Birr 30,000 to Birr 75,000 and set a daily aggregate transaction limit of Birr 150,000, with exemptions such as utility, tax and bulk payments. It also allows banks to set up dedicated mobile money subsidiaries.

scenario.title: The trader and the wallet
scenario.situation: Ato Kebede Worku sells clothes at the market and is paid by customers into his mobile wallet. He expects to receive about Birr 120,000 on some days before a holiday, and asks Hanna whether the wallet is enough.
scenario.question: What should Hanna advise?
options: The wallet is fine for any amount if he transfers quickly
Link the wallet to a bank account or receive larger payments directly into the account, since a wallet may hold at most Birr 75,000
Ask his customers to pay in cash instead
Open three wallets in family members' names
scenario.explain: The NBE wallet balance limit is Birr 75,000, so on busy days payments could fail. A linked bank account, or merchant payments into the account, has no such limit. Splitting across relatives' wallets is unsafe and may breach KYC rules.

lessons.title: Loans for individuals and small businesses
body: Branch staff do not approve loans, but customers ask them first. Common retail loans are personal or salary loans repaid from monthly salary, housing and vehicle loans, and small business loans for traders and micro and small enterprises. Each has eligibility rules, required documents, collateral or guarantee requirements and an approval process set by the bank's credit policy.

Your role is to explain the product honestly, give the document checklist, and pass the customer to the credit officer. Never promise approval, an amount or a rate before the bank has assessed the application.
When explaining a loan, always cover the total cost: interest, fees and the monthly installment the customer must pay. Module 3 shows how to explain the annual percentage rate (APR) simply.
points: Salary loans: employer letter, payslips, salary assignment to the bank
Business loans: trade licence, TIN, financial records or a simple business plan
Housing and vehicle loans: proforma or sale agreement, collateral documents
All loans: valid ID, a completed application and consent for a credit bureau check

example.title: A promise that backfired
example.text: A new officer told Weizerit Selam Tesfaye, a nurse, that her Birr 200,000 salary loan 'would surely be approved this week'. The credit assessment found an existing loan at another bank, and the bank approved Birr 120,000. Selam had already paid a deposit on furniture and complained that she was misled. The officer should have explained the documents and the steps, and said that the amount depends on the assessment of her repayment capacity.

lessons.tip: Say 'the credit team will assess your application and tell you the amount and terms' instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Remittance payout and diaspora customers
body: Millions of Ethiopian families receive money from relatives abroad through international money transfer operators. At the branch, the recipient presents the reference number, the sender's name and the expected amount, and a valid ID. The teller checks the details against the transfer message, pays in Birr at the bank's rate of the day or credits the recipient's account, and keeps the countersigned voucher.

Know your payee: the money goes only to the named recipient, after their identity is checked. A reference number alone is never enough, because references are shared, stolen and sold. If details do not match, the payment waits until they do.

Remittance recipients are ideal customers for an account. Crediting an account is safer than carrying cash home, and the family can save part of each transfer. Diaspora senders can also open foreign currency accounts in Ethiopia under the rules of FXD/01/2024.

items.label: Collect details
items.text: Reference, sender name, expected amount and country.

items.label: Check identity
items.text: Valid ID matching the recipient name on the message.

items.label: Match the message
items.text: Reference, names and amount agree with the transfer system.

items.label: Pay or credit
items.text: Birr at the day's rate, or credit to the recipient's account.

items.label: Record
items.text: Countersigned voucher, receipt to the customer.

worked.title: Remittance payout for Weizero Tigist Alemayehu (illustrative rate)

rows.label: Amount sent by her son in Washington
Illustrative bank buying rate of the day
Option 1: cash paid at the counter
Option 2: credited to a new savings account
rows.value: Birr 60,000, of which she withdraws Birr 15,000

rows.label: Left saving in the account under option 2

worked.note: Offering an account turns a one-time payout into a relationship and keeps most of the cash off the street.

lessons.title: Interest-free products
body: Many Ethiopian customers prefer banking that does not pay or charge interest, for religious or personal reasons. The NBE allows banks to offer interest-free banking through dedicated windows or as full-fledged interest-free banks, under Directive No. SBB/72/2019.

Common interest-free deposit products are wadiah (a safekeeping account where the bank guarantees the deposit and pays no return) and qard (a loan from the customer to the bank, repayable on demand), while mudarabah investment accounts share profit rather than pay a fixed rate. On the financing side, murabaha is a cost-plus sale: the bank buys the asset and sells it to the customer at a disclosed markup paid in installments.

Offer interest-free options to every customer, not only to those you assume want them. Explain the product in plain terms, including that a mudarabah return is not guaranteed and that a murabaha markup is a fixed, disclosed price.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/72/2019, Interest-free banking
regulation.text: The directive allows interest-free banking business through interest-free windows of conventional banks and through full-fledged interest-free banks. Interest-free products must be kept separate from conventional business, so staff should open them as their own product types, not as conventional accounts with the interest removed.

left.title: Conventional
items: Savings account pays interest
Loan charges interest on the balance
Return set by the bank's rate
Fixed deposit for a higher rate

right.title: Interest-free
items: Wadiah or qard account: safekeeping, no interest
Murabaha: asset sold at a disclosed markup
Mudarabah: profit shared, not guaranteed
Kept separate from conventional business

scenario.title: The assumption at the desk
scenario.situation: Ato Ahmed Mohammed, a shop owner in Dire Dawa, asks Hanna for 'the best savings account'. She notices his name and immediately offers only the interest-free wadiah account. Another customer, Weizero Rahel Getachew, asks the same question and Hanna offers only a fixed deposit.
scenario.question: What would have been better?
options: Hanna's approach is correct, since it saves time
Always offer the product with the highest bank margin
Ask customers about their religion before recommending
Ask each customer a few questions about their needs and preferences, and present both conventional and interest-free options
scenario.explain: Assumptions based on names are unfair and often wrong. Asking about needs and offering both types lets the customer choose, which is what fair treatment requires.

lessons.title: Matching products to needs
body: Matching starts with questions, not with a brochure. Ask what the customer wants to do with the money, how often they need access, how they receive and send money, and whether they prefer interest-free banking. Then recommend one or two products and explain why.

A good match solves the customer's problem and is affordable for them. A poor match, such as a fixed deposit for someone who needs the money next month, or a current account for someone who will never write a cheque, creates complaints later.
Record what the customer asked for and what you recommended. If they choose something else, that is their right; your duty is to make sure they understood the features, fees and risks.

items.label: Ask
items.text: What is the money for, and when will you need it?

items.label: Listen
items.text: Note income pattern, channels used, preferences.

items.label: Inform
items.text: Explain one or two options, with fees and limits.

items.label: Guide
items.text: Recommend the best fit and say why.

items.label: Note
items.text: Record the advice and the customer's choice.

example.title: Three customers, three products
example.text: In one morning at Kera branch, Hanna served a university student who receives Birr 3,000 a month from her parents (a savings account with mobile banking, so she can receive transfers without visiting), a carpenter saving for a machine he will buy in a year (a fixed time deposit for part of his savings, with the rest in savings) and an idir committee collecting monthly contributions (a group account with the by-laws and minutes naming the signatories).

scenario.title: The pensioner and the fixed deposit
scenario.situation: Ato Girma Desta, 72, has Birr 150,000 from selling a small plot of land. He lives on a monthly pension of Birr 4,200 and says he may need money for medical costs. A colleague suggests putting the whole amount in a 24-month fixed deposit for the best rate.
scenario.question: What should Hanna recommend?
options: Keep an emergency amount in savings and fix only the part he will not need, after explaining the early withdrawal penalty
The 24-month fixed deposit for the full Birr 150,000
A current account with a cheque book
Advise him to keep the cash at home
scenario.explain: A split keeps money available for medical needs while earning a better rate on the rest. Locking everything up risks penalties when he needs it; a cheque book does not fit his needs; cash at home is unsafe.

takeaways: Savings, current and fixed time deposits serve different needs; special accounts serve groups, minors, women and pensioners.
Banks set their own deposit and lending rates under NBE/INT/13/2026; quote the bank's published rate and never promise one.
Mobile wallets are limited to a Birr 75,000 balance and Birr 150,000 in daily transactions under ONPS/09/2023; larger flows belong in a bank account.
Pay remittances only to the named, identified recipient, and offer an account to keep the money safe.
Offer interest-free options under SBB/72/2019 to every customer and explain how they differ from conventional products.
Match products by asking about the customer's purpose, timing and preferences, then record the advice.

quiz.q: Under NBE/INT/13/2026, who sets savings deposit rates?
options: The NBE sets a minimum for all banks
The Ministry of Finance
Each bank, with board approval, reported to the NBE
The branch manager
quiz.explain: Banks set rates freely with board approval, and there is no NBE minimum savings rate.

quiz.q: A mobile wallet holds Birr 70,000. Under ONPS/09/2023, can it receive a further Birr 10,000?
options: No, the balance would exceed the Birr 75,000 limit
Yes, there is no limit
Yes, if it is a business wallet
Only on weekends
quiz.explain: Birr 80,000 would exceed the daily wallet balance limit of Birr 75,000.

quiz.q: What must be checked before paying an incoming remittance?
options: Only the reference number
The sender's passport
Nothing, if the customer is known
The recipient's valid ID and that the names, reference and amount match the transfer message
quiz.explain: Know your payee: identity and matching details, not just the reference.

quiz.q: In a murabaha financing, what does the customer pay?
options: Interest on the outstanding balance
A disclosed cost-plus price, usually in installments
A share of business profit
Nothing until the asset is sold
quiz.explain: Murabaha is a sale at an agreed markup disclosed at the start.

quiz.q: Birr 80,000 is placed in a 6-month fixed deposit at an illustrative 8% a year. What is the interest at maturity, before tax?
options: Birr 3,200
Birr 4,800
Birr 6,400
Birr 8,000

quiz.q: Which is the first step in matching a product to a customer?
options: Hand over the brochure
Offer the product with the best margin
Ask what the money is for and when it will be needed
Check the customer's religion
quiz.explain: Needs come first; products follow.

modules.title: Communication skills: listening, questioning and explaining costs
modules.summary: Listen actively, ask the right questions and explain fees, rates and the annual percentage rate clearly to customers of every language and literacy level.
objectives: Use active listening and open and closed questions to understand a customer's real need
Explain fees, interest and the annual percentage rate (APR) in plain words and numbers
Compare flat and declining-balance interest so customers understand the true cost
Adapt explanations for customers with low literacy or a different language, and explain a loan decline respectfully

lessons.title: Active listening
body: Most service failures start with a misunderstanding, not with bad intent. Active listening means giving full attention, letting the customer finish, and checking that you understood before you act. It is the fastest way to serve correctly, because it avoids doing the wrong transaction and starting again.

Show you are listening: face the customer, put the pen or mouse down, nod, and use short signals such as 'yes, I understand'. Then summarize: 'So you sent Birr 8,000 to your brother in Bahir Dar yesterday and he has not received it, is that right?'
Listen for feelings as well as facts. A customer who says 'this is the third time I have come' is telling you they are tired and losing trust. Acknowledge that first, then solve the problem.

items.label: Attend
items.text: Full attention, eye contact, no distractions.

items.label: Let them finish
items.text: Do not interrupt or jump to the answer.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.text: Name the feeling: 'I can see this has been stressful.'

items.label: Summarize
items.text: Repeat the key facts in your own words.

items.label: Confirm
items.text: 'Is that right?' before you act.

example.title: The wrong account
example.text: A trader told Dawit he wanted to 'put money in the account'. Dawit deposited Birr 35,000 into the trader's savings account. The trader meant his supplier's account at the same bank, and the supplier stopped deliveries for a day while the reversal was approved. Ten seconds of summarizing, 'You want to deposit Birr 35,000 into your own savings account?', would have avoided the error.

lessons.title: Asking the right questions
body: Open questions start with what, how, why or tell me, and invite the customer to explain: 'What would you like to use the account for?' Closed questions have short answers and confirm facts: 'Is the account in your name?' Use open questions to explore and closed questions to confirm.

Avoid questions that sound like accusations, such as 'Why didn't you bring your ID?' Instead ask, 'Do you have your ID with you today? If not, I can tell you what we need.' Avoid asking for information you do not need; customers are right to be wary of questions about their family or income without a reason.
When the customer's need is unclear, use a funnel: start with an open question, narrow with more specific ones, and close with a confirmation.

left.title: Open questions
items: What brings you to the branch today?
How do you usually receive your income?
Tell me what happened with the transfer.
What matters most to you in an account?

right.title: Closed questions
items: Is this your own account?
Was the amount Birr 8,000?
Did you receive an SMS?
Shall I proceed with the transfer?

scenario.title: The vague request
scenario.situation: A young man tells Hanna, 'I want to do something with my money so it grows.' He works at a nearby factory and earns Birr 9,000 a month.
scenario.question: Which question should Hanna ask first?
options: 'Do you want a fixed deposit?'
'How much do you have in total, including what your family has?'
'What are you hoping to use the money for, and when might you need it?'
'Why have you not saved before?'
scenario.explain: An open question about purpose and timing reveals the need. Jumping to a product, asking intrusive questions or sounding critical all close the conversation.

lessons.title: Explaining fees, rates and the APR
body: Customers often compare loans only by the interest rate. But fees paid at the start, such as a service or commitment fee, raise the true cost. The annual percentage rate (APR) puts interest and fees together as one yearly percentage, so customers can compare offers fairly.

Explain in three steps: what the customer receives, what they repay in total, and what that costs per year. Use Birr amounts, not only percentages. Many customers understand 'you will pay Birr 10,800 for borrowing this money for one year' far better than '16% plus 2% fee'.
Disclosure is a legal duty, not only good practice. Give the customer the written terms, point to the fees and the APR, and let them take time to decide.

regulation.source: NBE Financial Consumer Protection Directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported)
regulation.text: As reported, the NBE's consumer protection directive requires banks to treat customers fairly, to disclose the terms and costs of products clearly, including loan costs expressed as an annual percentage rate, to handle complaints and to protect customer data. Rates themselves are set by each bank under NBE/INT/13/2026.

worked.title: One-year loan for Ato Yonas Tadesse: rate versus APR (illustrative terms)

rows.label: Interest at 16% for one year, repaid at the end
Service fee of 2%, deducted at the start
Cost per year on the money received (10,800 / 58,800)

worked.note: The rate says 16%, but the true yearly cost, the APR, is about 18.4%. Tell Yonas both, in Birr and in percent.

lessons.tip: Write the key numbers on a slip for the customer: what you receive, what you repay, and the yearly cost.

lessons.title: Flat and declining-balance interest
body: Some lenders, especially in informal and microfinance lending, quote a flat rate: interest is charged on the original amount for the whole term, even though the customer repays part of it every month. Banks usually charge interest on the declining balance: each month's interest is on what is still owed.

The same rate number gives a very different cost. A flat rate looks cheaper in conversation but costs almost twice as much in interest as the same declining-balance rate on a one-year loan with monthly installments.
When a customer compares your offer with another lender's, ask how the other lender calculates interest. Showing the Birr total for both is the clearest answer.

worked.title: Birr 60,000 over 12 monthly installments at 15% (illustrative)

rows.label: Flat: interest on the original amount (60,000 x 15%)
Declining balance: monthly installment (1.25% a month)
Declining balance: total interest (5,415.50 x 12 minus 60,000)
Extra interest paid under the flat method

worked.note: A 15% flat rate costs the customer about Birr 4,000 more than 15% on the declining balance.

visual.caption: Own worked example: Birr 60,000 over 12 months.

example.title: Selam compares two offers
example.text: Weizerit Selam Tesfaye was offered a Birr 60,000 loan at '15% flat' by an informal lender and at 15% declining balance by the bank. She almost chose the lender because 'the rate is the same and they are faster'. Hanna wrote both installments and totals on a slip: Birr 5,750 a month against about Birr 5,415. Selam saw she would save about Birr 4,000 and applied at the bank.

lessons.title: Different languages and literacy levels
body: Ethiopia has more than 80 languages, and many customers read little or not at all. Serving them well is part of financial inclusion. Speak the customer's language where possible, use simple words, short sentences and real Birr amounts, and avoid banking terms such as 'principal', 'maturity' or 'debit' unless you explain them.

For customers who cannot read, read out the key terms of any form before they sign or give a thumbprint, and follow the bank's procedure: many banks take the thumbprint before a witness and a bank officer, and place a photo on the passbook. Check understanding by asking the customer to say back what they agreed to, not by asking 'Do you understand?'
Use pictures and objects: show the passbook entries, point to the amounts on the receipt, and use the ATM or phone together with the customer the first time.

items.label: Their language
items.text: Find a colleague if you do not speak it.

items.label: Birr, not percent
items.text: Real amounts are easier than rates.

items.label: Read it out
items.text: Key terms read aloud before signing.

items.label: Teach back
items.text: Ask the customer to say it in their words.

scenario.title: The fee notice
scenario.situation: Weizero Zenebech Abebe, a pensioner who reads little, holds up a notice about a new SMS alert fee and asks why money left her account. She speaks Amharic.
scenario.question: What is the best response?
options: Hand her the printed fee schedule to read
Explain in simple Amharic what the alert is, how much it costs each month in Birr, and offer to stop it if she does not want it
Tell her all customers pay this fee and nothing can be done
Ask her to come back with a grandchild who can read
scenario.explain: A plain explanation in Birr, in her language, with a real choice, respects her and meets disclosure duties. A written schedule or a refusal to explain fails her.

lessons.title: Explaining a loan rejection
body: Telling a customer that their loan was declined is one of the hardest branch moments. Done badly, it ends the relationship. Done well, the customer leaves with dignity, understands why, and knows what they could do next.

Meet in private, not across a busy counter. Give the decision clearly and early, then the main reason in plain words, such as 'your current monthly repayments already take a large share of your salary'. Do not blame the customer, the credit team or the system, and do not share internal scores or other customers' information.
End with a next step: a smaller amount, a guarantor, a savings plan to build a deposit, or reapplying after an existing loan is repaid. Record the conversation.

items.label: Private setting
items.text: A desk or room, not the open counter.

items.label: Clear decision
items.text: Say it early and kindly.

items.label: Main reason
items.text: One or two reasons in plain words.

items.label: Next step
items.text: What could change the answer in future.

items.label: Record
items.text: Note what was explained and the customer's reaction.

scenario.title: Ato Bekele's loan
scenario.situation: Ato Bekele Tsegaye, a minibus owner, applied for a Birr 400,000 loan to buy a second vehicle. The credit team declined because his existing loan installments already take most of his net income. He arrives at the counter and asks loudly in front of others, 'Did my loan come out?'
scenario.question: What should Hanna do?
options: Tell him at the counter that the credit team rejected him
Say the system is down and ask him to come back next week
Give him a copy of the internal credit assessment
Invite him to a private desk, explain the decision and the main reason in plain words, and discuss what could make a future application possible
scenario.explain: Privacy and a clear reason with a way forward keep his dignity and the relationship. Announcing it publicly, delaying with an untrue excuse or handing over internal documents are all wrong.

takeaways: Active listening and a quick summary prevent most errors and repeat visits.
Use open questions to explore needs and closed questions to confirm facts; never sound accusing.
Explain the total cost in Birr and as an APR, including fees deducted at the start.
A flat rate costs far more than the same declining-balance rate; show both totals.
For low-literacy customers, use their language, real amounts, read the terms aloud and check with teach-back.
Explain a loan decline privately, clearly, with the main reason and a next step.

quiz.q: A Birr 100,000 one-year loan at 14% interest has a 1% fee deducted at the start. What does the customer receive?
options: Birr 86,000
Birr 99,000
quiz.explain: 100,000 minus the Birr 1,000 fee = Birr 99,000.

quiz.q: In the same loan, what is the APR, approximately?
Which is an open question?
options: Is this your account?
Did you get an SMS?
How do you usually receive your income?
Is the amount Birr 5,000?
quiz.explain: It invites the customer to explain.

quiz.q: Why does a flat rate cost more than the same declining-balance rate?
options: Interest is charged on the original amount even after part is repaid
Flat rates are always higher numbers
Flat loans have longer terms
Fees are added each month
quiz.explain: The customer pays interest on money already repaid.

quiz.q: What is the best way to check that a low-literacy customer understood the terms?
options: Ask 'Do you understand?'
Give them the brochure
Ask for a signature
Ask the customer to explain the key terms back in their own words
quiz.explain: Teach-back shows real understanding.

quiz.q: When explaining a loan decline, which should you avoid?
options: Meeting in private
Sharing the internal credit score and blaming the credit team
Giving the main reason in plain words
Suggesting a next step
quiz.explain: Internal scores stay internal, and blaming colleagues damages trust in the bank.

modules.title: Serving all customers fairly and compliance at the counter
modules.summary: Serve women, elders, persons with disabilities, rural and diaspora customers with equal respect, and protect customers and the bank through KYC, cash handling, counterfeit checks, confidentiality and fraud alerts.
objectives: Identify the needs of women, elderly customers, persons with disabilities, rural and diaspora customers, and adjust service without discrimination
Apply KYC steps at the counter, including when a remittance recipient has no ID
Handle cash, counterfeit notes and till differences by the procedure
Protect customer data and recognize common fraud signs

lessons.title: Fair treatment and vulnerable customers
body: Fair treatment means that every customer receives the same respect, the same information and the same rules, whatever their gender, age, disability, language, religion, ethnicity or wealth. It does not mean serving everyone identically: a customer who cannot see, hear or read needs different support to reach the same outcome.

Some customers are more vulnerable to poor service or abuse: elders who depend on relatives, customers with limited literacy, persons with disabilities, people in distress after a bereavement, and new customers from rural areas. Watch for signs of pressure, such as a relative who answers every question or insists on a large withdrawal.

Ethiopia's National Financial Inclusion Strategy (NFIS-II) puts special weight on reaching women, rural people and others left out of formal finance. Every respectful, clear transaction at the counter is part of meeting that goal.

regulation.source: NBE Financial Consumer Protection Directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported)
regulation.text: As reported, the directive requires fair treatment and non-discrimination, special care for vulnerable customers, clear disclosure and complaint handling. Ethiopian law also protects the rights of persons with disabilities. In practice, a branch must make its services usable for all customers and must not refuse or delay service on grounds such as gender, age or disability.

items.label: Women
items.text: Serve in their own right; never require a husband's presence unless the product rules do.

items.label: Elders
items.text: Seating, patience, priority where the bank allows, watch for pressure.

items.label: Persons with disabilities
items.text: Ramp or desk service, read aloud, thumbprint with witness.

items.label: Rural customers
items.text: Plain language, their language, explain the passbook and receipts.

items.label: Diaspora
items.text: Clear FCY account rules, remote service, remittance follow-up.

example.title: The account opened in her own name
example.text: Weizero Meseret Lemma, a seller of injera from a village near Sendafa, came to Kera branch to open a savings account. A staff member asked her to bring her husband to sign. Meron corrected this immediately: an adult woman opens an account in her own name with her own ID. Meseret opened the account that day and now saves Birr 1,500 every week.

lessons.title: Serving persons with disabilities and elderly customers in practice
body: Small changes make the branch usable for everyone: a ramp or a ground-floor desk, chairs in the waiting area, a lower counter or a staff member who comes out from behind it, and a queue priority where the bank's policy allows. Speak directly to the customer, not to their companion.

For a visually impaired customer, read documents aloud, guide their hand to the signature or thumbprint place, and follow the bank's procedure: many banks take the thumbprint before a witness and a bank officer, put a photo on the passbook and have a supervisor authorize each transaction. For a deaf customer, write notes or use a colleague who knows Ethiopian Sign Language.
Never decide for a customer what they can or cannot do. Offer help and let them accept or decline it.

scenario.title: The wheelchair at the steps
scenario.situation: Ato Tesfaye Mulugeta uses a wheelchair and cannot climb the four steps at Kera branch's entrance. He calls the branch from outside to say he wants to withdraw Birr 6,000 from his savings account.
scenario.question: What should the branch do?
options: Ask him to send a relative with a written authorization
Send a teller with a supervisor to serve him at the entrance with the proper ID check and receipt, and report the access problem to the branch manager
Tell him to use the ATM, which is also up the steps
Ask the guard to carry him up the steps
scenario.explain: Bringing the service to him, under normal controls, serves him now; reporting the steps leads to a lasting fix. The other options shift the burden to him or are unsafe.

lessons.title: KYC at the counter
body: Know your customer (KYC) means identifying every customer, verifying who they are with a valid document and understanding what transactions are normal for them. It protects customers from fraud and the bank from being used for money laundering. KYC applies when opening an account, when paying remittances and cashier's payment orders, and for large or unusual transactions.

Acceptable IDs include a kebele ID, the Fayda national digital ID, a passport or a driving licence, as set in the bank's procedure. Check that the ID is valid and not expired, that the photo matches the person, and that the name matches the account or the remittance message.

When something does not fit, such as a cash deposit far above the customer's usual pattern, a customer who refuses to say where funds come from, or several people depositing small amounts into one account, follow the bank's procedure and report to the compliance unit. Do not tell the customer that you are reporting.

regulation.source: NBE KYC/CDD directive (2021, number to confirm; as reported)
regulation.text: As reported, the directive requires banks to identify and verify customers, assess their risk, and monitor transactions, with enhanced checks for higher-risk customers. It works with the anti-money laundering law and the Financial Intelligence Service's reporting rules. At the counter, this means no payment or account without verified identity.

scenario.title: The remittance without ID
scenario.situation: A young woman says her uncle in Dubai sent her Birr 18,000 through a money transfer operator. She has the reference number and the sender's name, which match the message, but she left her ID at home. She is upset and says the money is for her mother's medicine today.
scenario.question: What should Dawit do?
options: Pay her, since the reference and sender name match
Pay half now and the rest when she brings the ID
Pay her if she gives her mother's phone number
Explain kindly that the money is safe and can only be paid after her identity is checked, and tell her exactly which IDs are accepted so she can return today
scenario.explain: Know your payee requires a valid ID; references are often shared or stolen. Explaining that the money is safe, and exactly what to bring, keeps the customer's trust while keeping the rule.

lessons.title: Cash handling and counterfeit notes
body: Cash work is still central in Ethiopian branches. Count every deposit in front of the customer against the denominations on the slip, and give the system receipt as the customer's proof. For withdrawals, check the voucher, the signature and the ID, and count the cash twice, once to yourself and once to the customer.

Check notes for security features under good light: the watermark, the security thread, raised print and the feel of the paper. If you find a suspected counterfeit, do not return it to the customer. Explain calmly, give a receipt for the retained note, credit only the genuine notes and follow the bank's reporting procedure. The customer is not accused; many people receive fake notes without knowing.
At the end of the day every till must balance. A difference is reported to the supervisor immediately, never covered from personal money or hidden until the next day.

regulation.source: National Bank of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1359/2025 (legal tender and currency provisions, as taught in Erudite's Domestic Banking Operations course)
regulation.text: Counterfeit notes must be reported and must not be put back into circulation. Coins are legal tender only up to Birr 10 per payment unless the parties agree otherwise, and the NBE sets cash withdrawal and holding limits. Crypto payments are not allowed.

worked.title: Dawit's till at the close of business (Birr)

rows.label: Opening cash received from the head till
Suspected counterfeit Birr 200 note retained from a deposit of 25,000 (only 24,800 credited)
rows.value: Not in till; held with receipt

worked.note: The counterfeit note does not explain the shortage because only Birr 24,800 was credited. Dawit reports the Birr 500 shortage to the supervisor at once for investigation, and the counterfeit goes through the reporting procedure.

example.title: The counterfeit in the bundle
example.text: A wholesaler's employee deposited Birr 25,000 at Kera branch. Dawit found one Birr 200 note with no clear watermark and a printed, not embedded, thread. He showed the employee the difference against a genuine note, retained it with a receipt, credited Birr 24,800 and called the supervisor. The employee was annoyed at first, but thanked Dawit after seeing the features, and the wholesaler bought a note checker for the shop.

lessons.title: Customer confidentiality and data protection
body: Customer information belongs to the customer. Balances, transactions, loan details, addresses and phone numbers are shared only with the customer, with people they have authorized in writing, or where the law requires it, such as a court order. This includes spouses, parents, employers and friends.

Ethiopia's Personal Data Protection Proclamation (No. 1321/2024, as reported) sets rules for collecting and using personal data: collect only what is needed for a stated purpose, keep it secure, use it only for that purpose and respect customers' rights over their data. At the counter, this means no customer data on personal phones, no screens visible to the queue, no documents left on the desk and no discussing customers in public.
Phone calls are a common risk. Never confirm balances or account details to a caller you cannot verify, even if they sound official or know some details.

regulation.source: Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024 (as reported)
regulation.text: The proclamation governs the collection and processing of personal data. Banks should collect personal data for a clear and lawful purpose, keep it accurate and secure, limit access to staff who need it, and not disclose it without a lawful basis. Branch staff should follow the bank's data procedures and report any breach at once.

scenario.title: The husband on the phone
scenario.situation: A caller says he is the husband of Weizero Hiwot Assefa, a Kera branch customer. He gives her full name and account number and asks Hanna for her current balance, saying they are planning to buy a house together.
scenario.question: What should Hanna do?
options: Politely decline, explain that account information is given only to the account holder or a person she has authorized in writing, and invite Hiwot to contact the branch
Give the balance, since he knows the account number
Give an approximate balance only
Ask him for his own ID number and then give the balance
scenario.explain: Knowing an account number does not authorize access. Only the customer or a written authorization does; even a rough figure is a breach.

lessons.title: Fraud alerts at the counter
body: Fraudsters target both customers and staff. Common schemes in Ethiopia include callers pretending to be bank staff who ask for a PIN or one-time code, fake messages about lottery wins or delivered goods, impostors with forged IDs trying to withdraw from someone else's account, and pressure on elderly customers by people posing as relatives or officials.

Watch for warning signs: a customer withdrawing an unusual amount while on the phone with someone giving instructions, a person who knows little about the account they claim to own, an ID with signs of alteration, or a customer anxious to send money urgently to someone they have never met. Pause, ask gentle questions and involve the supervisor.

Teach customers three rules: the bank will never ask for your PIN or code, check before you send, and call the branch on the official number if in doubt. The NBE also expects microfinance institutions to run customer fraud awareness campaigns (Instruction FCPED/142/26, April 2026), which shows how seriously it views customer fraud.

items.label: Spot
items.text: Notice unusual amounts, pressure or mismatched details.

items.label: Talk
items.text: Ask gentle questions about the purpose.

items.label: Own it
items.text: Pause the transaction if something is wrong.

items.label: Pass it up
items.text: Call the supervisor and follow the reporting procedure.

example.title: The urgent transfer
example.text: Ato Haile Gebru, 68, asked to transfer Birr 90,000 to an account in another city while a caller on speaker told him what to say. The caller claimed to be from a 'bank head office' fixing a problem with his pension. Hanna asked Haile to end the call, explained that the bank never asks customers to move money to fix an account, and called the supervisor. The transfer did not go ahead, and the fraud team blocked the receiving account details.

takeaways: Fair treatment means equal respect and outcomes; adjust the support, not the rules, for each customer.
Watch for vulnerable customers and signs of pressure from companions or callers.
No payment, remittance or account without verified ID; explain the rule kindly and say exactly what to bring.
Retain suspected counterfeit notes with a receipt, credit only genuine notes and report any till difference at once.
Customer data is shared only with the customer, a written authorized person or under the law; never by phone to an unverified caller.
Spot, talk, own it and pass it up when fraud signs appear.

quiz.q: A woman wants to open a savings account in her own name. A colleague says she needs her husband's signature. What is correct?
options: An adult woman opens an account in her own name with her own ID
She needs her husband's signature
She needs a guarantor
She can open only a joint account
quiz.explain: Requiring a husband's signature for her own account is discrimination.

quiz.q: A remittance recipient has the correct reference number but no ID. What should the teller do?
options: Pay because the reference matches
Pay a smaller amount
Explain the money is safe and pay after ID is presented
Return the money to the sender
quiz.explain: Know your payee requires verified identity.

quiz.q: Expected till cash is Birr 412,600 and counted cash is Birr 412,900. What is the position?
options: Birr 300 over
Birr 300 short
Balanced
Birr 3,000 over
quiz.explain: Counted cash exceeds expected by Birr 300, an overage that must also be reported.

quiz.q: What should a teller do with a suspected counterfeit note found in a deposit?
options: Return it to the customer
Accept it and report later
Destroy it
Retain it with a receipt, credit only genuine notes and report it
quiz.explain: Counterfeits must not go back into circulation and must be reported.

quiz.q: A caller knows a customer's account number and asks for the balance. What should you do?
options: Give the balance
Decline politely and ask the account holder to contact the branch
Give a rough figure
Ask for his address
quiz.explain: Knowing an account number is not authorization.

quiz.q: An elderly customer is withdrawing a large sum while a caller instructs him. What is the first step?
options: Complete the transaction quickly
Refuse service permanently
Pause, ask gentle questions and involve the supervisor
Ask the caller for ID
quiz.explain: Pausing protects the customer while you check for fraud.

modules.title: Complaints, difficult situations and the ten branch moments
modules.summary: Handle complaints through a clear process with timelines, escalation and records, calm angry customers, and bring every skill together in the ten branch moment role plays scored with a service rubric.
objectives: Follow a complaint process from receipt to resolution, with timelines, escalation and records
Calm an angry customer using a structured approach
Handle common branch problems such as failed transfers and captured cards
Perform the ten branch moment role plays and score them with a service rubric

lessons.title: Why complaints matter
body: A complaint is a customer telling the bank what went wrong while there is still time to fix it. Most unhappy customers never complain; they simply leave. A complaint handled well often makes the customer more loyal than before.

Complaints are also the bank's best free data. A pattern of complaints about failed transfers, long queues or unexplained fees points to a problem that one apology will not solve. That is why every complaint, however small, is recorded.

The NBE expects every bank to have a complaint-handling process that customers can use easily, that gives them an answer within set timelines and that tells them where to go if they are not satisfied.

regulation.source: NBE Financial Consumer Protection Directive (FCP/01/2020, as reported)
regulation.text: As reported, the directive requires banks to set up a complaint-handling procedure, to record and resolve complaints within set timelines, to tell customers how to escalate, and to report on complaints. Follow your bank's own procedure for the exact timelines; Bank A's procedure, used in this course, is an example, not the law.

items.label: ATM card captured or cash not dispensed

visual.caption: Own worked example: Kera branch complaint log, one month, 40 complaints.

example.title: What the log showed
example.text: Meron sorted Kera branch's 40 complaints for one month. Failed or delayed transfers were the largest group at 14, and most came from customers who had typed the wrong account number on mobile banking. The branch began showing customers how to check the payee name before confirming, and the next month transfer complaints fell to 8.

lessons.title: The complaint process: receive, record, resolve, respond
body: Every complaint follows the same path. Receive it politely wherever it arrives: at the counter, by phone, in writing or through the call center. Record it in the complaint register or system with the date, the customer's details, what happened and what they want. Give the customer a reference number.

Resolve it at the front line when you can, for example by correcting an error or explaining a fee. Escalate when you cannot: to the supervisor, then the branch manager, then the head office complaint unit. Respond to the customer within the bank's timeline, in a language they understand, with the outcome and the reason.

Close the complaint only when the customer has been told the outcome. If they are not satisfied, tell them how to escalate further, including to the NBE's consumer protection channel where the bank's process is exhausted.

items.label: Receive
items.text: Listen, thank, do not argue.

items.label: Record
items.text: Register details and give a reference number.

items.label: Resolve or escalate
items.text: Fix at the front line or pass up with the file.

items.label: Respond
items.text: Tell the customer the outcome and reason, on time.

items.label: Close and learn
items.text: Close only after the reply; review patterns monthly.

worked.title: Bank A's complaint timeline (an example procedure, not the law)

rows.label: Acknowledge and give a reference number
Escalation to branch manager if unresolved
Head office complaint unit for complex cases
Kera case: failed transfer reported on a Monday
Final reply due under the procedure, with no public holidays in the period

worked.note: Fifteen working days from a Monday ends on the Monday three weeks later; any public holiday pushes it back a day. Calendar the date and call the customer before it, even if only to report progress.

lessons.title: Calming angry customers
body: Anger is usually a mix of a real problem and a feeling of being ignored or treated unfairly. You cannot solve the problem until the feeling has been heard. Stay calm, keep your voice low and slow, and do not take the words personally.

Use the HEARD steps: hear them out without interrupting, empathize, apologize for the experience (not necessarily admitting fault), resolve or explain the next step, and diagnose the cause afterwards. Move the conversation away from the queue to a desk if possible; an audience makes people louder.
Know your limits. If a customer becomes threatening, call the supervisor or security. Your safety and that of other customers comes first.

items.label: Hear
items.text: Let them speak fully, without interrupting.

items.label: Empathize
items.text: 'I understand why you are upset.'

items.label: Apologize
items.text: 'I am sorry this happened to you.'

items.label: Resolve
items.text: Fix it, or give a clear next step and time.

items.label: Diagnose
items.text: Afterwards, find and fix the cause.

scenario.title: The card in the ATM
scenario.situation: Ato Dereje Fikru shouts at the counter that the ATM has taken his card and he needs cash for a funeral today. He demands to see the manager and says the bank is useless. Fifteen people in the queue are watching.
scenario.question: What should Hanna do first?
options: Tell him to lower his voice or leave
Invite him to her desk, let him explain, acknowledge the urgency and his loss, then check his ID and the bank's procedure for captured cards and a counter withdrawal
Call security immediately
Tell him captured cards take a week and he must wait
scenario.explain: Moving him away from the audience and hearing him out lowers the tension. A counter withdrawal with ID can meet his urgent need while the card is recovered or replaced under the procedure. Security is for threats, not for anger.

lessons.title: Common branch problems: failed transfers and system outages
body: A failed or delayed transfer is the most frequent complaint in many branches. The customer usually sees money leave their account but the payee has not received it. Check the transaction in the system: was it completed, pending, reversed or sent to a wrong account? Explain what you see in plain words.

If the money is pending or reversed, tell the customer when it should arrive or return, and follow up. If it went to a wrong account because of an error, start the bank's recovery procedure and be honest that recovery depends on the receiving account holder or bank. Never promise a time you cannot control.

During system outages, tell waiting customers honestly what is happening and offer alternatives such as the ATM or coming back at a specific time. Manual tickets are used only under the bank's outage procedure and must be replaced by system receipts later.

scenario.title: Debited but not received
scenario.situation: Weizero Hirut Yohannes sent Birr 8,000 by mobile banking to her brother's account at another bank on Friday. Her account was debited, but on Monday her brother still has nothing. She has come to the branch for the second time.
scenario.question: What should Hanna do?
options: Tell her it is the other bank's problem
Credit Birr 8,000 back to her account immediately from branch funds
Ask her to come back next week
Check the transaction status, record a complaint with a reference number, explain what happens next and when she will hear back, and follow up before that time
scenario.explain: Checking, recording and committing to a follow-up date resolves the issue properly. Blaming the other bank or sending her away fails her; crediting without investigation breaks controls.

lessons.title: Capstone: the ten branch moments
body: The capstone brings the course together in role plays of ten common moments at Kera branch. Working in threes, one learner plays the staff member, one the customer and one the observer, who scores with the service rubric. Rotate roles so everyone serves at least three moments.

Each moment tests a mix of skills: greeting and respect, listening and questioning, product and rule knowledge, clear explanation, compliance and the right escalation. The observer looks for the behaviors, not for perfect words.
After each role play, the observer gives two strengths and one improvement, and the group agrees what the rule requires. Prepare by reviewing your notebook from Modules 1 to 4.
points: 2. A trader choosing between an account and a mobile wallet (Module 2)
3. A pensioner who cannot read a fee notice (Module 3)
4. Explaining a loan rejection to a minibus owner (Module 3)
6. A wheelchair user who cannot reach the counter (Module 4)
7. A suspected counterfeit note in a deposit (Module 4)
8. A caller asking for a spouse's balance (Module 4)
9. A failed transfer, debited but not received (Module 5)
10. An angry customer whose card the ATM captured (Module 5)

example.title: Moment 5 in practice
example.text: In one practice round, a learner playing Dawit paid the remittance after the 'customer' cried and promised to bring her ID later. The observer scored the greeting and empathy highly but marked a compliance failure, so the role play failed regardless of the other scores. In the second attempt, the learner showed the same empathy, explained that the money was safe, listed the accepted IDs and offered to keep the transaction ready for her return that afternoon. It passed.

lessons.title: The service rubric and the assessment
body: The rubric scores five criteria from 1 to 5, each with a weight. Compliance carries the most weight and is also a gate: a role play that breaks a rule, such as paying without ID or disclosing a balance to a third party, fails whatever the other scores.

The pass mark for each role play is 70%, the same as for the course. The Level 1 certificate combines a knowledge test (60%), the role-play rubric (30%) and participation (10%), with a minimum of 80% attendance in the classroom version.
Use the rubric on yourself back at the branch. Once a week, pick one real interaction and score it honestly; the habit builds the skills faster than any course.

worked.title: Rubric score for Hanna in moment 9, the failed transfer

rows.label: Accuracy and compliance (weight 30%): score 3 of 5, no breach

worked.note: Hanna passes. Her improvement point: she checked the transaction but forgot to give the reference number until the customer asked.

scenario.title: Scoring a compliance breach
scenario.situation: In moment 8, a learner greets the caller warmly, listens well and is polite throughout, scoring 5 on four criteria. At the end, to be helpful, the learner tells the caller that the balance is 'more than Birr 100,000'.
scenario.question: How should the observer score the role play?
options: Fail, because disclosing even an approximate balance to an unverified third party is a compliance breach
Pass, with a weighted score above 90%
Pass, since no exact figure was given
Score it as a draw and repeat later
scenario.explain: The compliance gate overrides the other scores. An approximate balance is still customer information disclosed without authorization.

takeaways: Complaints are early warnings and free data; record every one.
Receive, record, resolve or escalate, respond and close: give a reference number and meet the timeline.
Calm anger with HEARD, away from the queue, and call security only for threats.
For failed transfers, check the status, record, explain the next step and follow up before the promised time.
The capstone tests ten branch moments with a weighted rubric, a 70% pass mark and a compliance gate.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do when a complaint arrives at the counter?
options: Decide who is at fault
Send the customer to head office
Listen, thank the customer and record the complaint with a reference number
Ask for it in writing
quiz.explain: Receive politely and record; fault comes later.

quiz.q: In HEARD, what does the A stand for?
options: Apologize
Argue
Approve
Audit
quiz.explain: Apologize for the experience, which is not necessarily admitting fault.

quiz.q: A rubric gives weights 10%, 20%, 30%, 20%, 20% and scores 4, 4, 4, 3, 3 out of 5. What is the percentage?
When should a complaint be closed?
options: When it is recorded
When the branch manager has seen it
After one week
When the customer has been told the outcome and reason
quiz.explain: Closing before the customer is told leaves them without an answer.

quiz.q: A customer's transfer is pending. What should you avoid?
options: Explaining the status in plain words
Promising a time you cannot control
Recording the complaint
Agreeing a follow-up date
quiz.explain: Promise only what the bank controls, and follow up.

quiz.q: Which behavior automatically fails a role play?
options: A slow greeting
Forgetting the customer's name
Paying a remittance without verified ID
Taking notes
quiz.explain: Compliance breaches fail the role play regardless of other scores.

simulation.title: A week as customer service supervisor at Bank A, Bishoftu branch
setting: You have just been made customer service supervisor at Bank A's Bishoftu branch, a busy town branch that serves factory workers from the industrial park, flower farm staff, traders, pensioners and families who receive money from relatives abroad. The hall has 6 teller windows, 3 customer service desks and 2 ATMs, and it fills before opening on salary days.

You lead the hall: the tellers, the customer service officers and the greeter at the door. You report to the branch manager, Ato Fikadu Tessema. Your job this week is to keep the queue under control, help customers choose products that fit them, explain costs honestly, protect every customer's money and data, and handle complaints by the procedure.

Each item arrives in the order it reaches you. Read the facts, do the numbers yourself, and choose what you would actually do and say at the counter, knowing the branch manager, the compliance unit and the customer will all judge the result.

authority.title: Your hall's rules and promises

rows.label: Bank A service promises (example)
rows.value: Greet within one minute; explain every fee before the customer signs; never say "come back tomorrow" without a reason and a time; call back the same day on every promise

rows.label: Rates and loans
rows.value: Quote only the bank's board-approved, published rates (NBE/INT/13/2026); never promise a rate, an amount or a loan approval

rows.label: Disclosure
rows.value: Explain total cost in Birr and as an APR, including fees deducted at the start (FCP/01/2020, as reported)

rows.label: Mobile wallets
rows.value: Balance up to Birr 75,000; daily transactions up to Birr 150,000, with exemptions (ONPS/09/2023)

rows.label: KYC and remittances
rows.value: No account, payment or remittance without verified ID; pay remittances only to the named recipient

rows.label: Confidentiality
rows.value: Account information only to the customer, a person authorized in writing, or where the law requires (Proclamation No. 1321/2024, as reported)

rows.label: Interest-free products
rows.value: Opened as their own product types, kept separate from conventional business (SBB/72/2019)

rows.label: Bank A complaint timeline (example)
rows.value: Reference number same day; front-line resolution within 2 working days; branch manager on day 3; final reply within 15 working days

authority.note: These follow the course. Bank A's promises and timelines are examples, not the law: your own institution's policy and procedures always come first.

meters.label: Customer trust
meters.help: Rises when customers are treated with respect and understand what was done; falls with rudeness, confusion or broken promises.

meters.label: Compliance
meters.help: Falls sharply with any breach of KYC, confidentiality, disclosure or the bank's procedures, however kind the intention.

meters.label: Accounts and deposits
meters.help: Rises when customers open accounts, save and stay; falls when they leave or are lost to a poor match.

meters.label: Queue and speed
meters.help: Rises when the hall flows and work is right the first time; falls with long waits, rework and repeat visits.

tasks.subject: Salary day: two tellers want their break at 08:30
body: It is the industrial park's salary day. At the morning huddle, two tellers who came in early ask to take their tea break together at 08:30. The branch manager asks for your plan for the 08:00 to 10:00 peak.
Last month's count showed that about one customer in four at the windows only wanted a balance check or a mini statement, which the ATMs and mobile banking can do.

rows.label: Share of window customers who only need a balance or mini statement

options.text: Keep all 6 windows open to 10:00, move breaks after the peak, and have the greeter send balance requests to the ATMs, cutting arrivals to about 72 an hour.
options.outcome: Correct: each window serves 60 / 5 = 12 an hour, so 6 windows serve 72. Moving one in four customers to the ATM brings arrivals down to 72 and the queue stops growing. Breaks still happen, just outside the peak.
